c.tagline: Andes-backed metropolis of wine and culture

emergency.note: Fire is 132; operators rarely speak English, so ask a local or your hotel to call.

hood_landmark.Providencia: Sky Costanera observation deck atop Gran Torre Santiago
hood_landmark.Las Condes: the gleaming 'Sanhattan' El Golf skyscraper district
hood_landmark.Bellavista: La Chascona, Pablo Neruda's house at the foot of Cerro San Cristóbal
hood_landmark.Nunoa: Estadio Nacional, Chile's national stadium and memorial site

avoid.reason: Avoid La Legua, La Pintana and the southern comunas.
Pickpocketing in the centre, Bellavista and Plaza de Armas; caution near Plaza Baquedano during protests.

hood_desc: A central, upscale district with tree-lined avenues, cafes, shopping and good metro links; suits first-time visitors and business travelers wanting a safe, walkable, well-connected base.
A modern, affluent business and financial district nicknamed Sanhattan, with skyscrapers, malls and upscale hotels; suits business travelers and those wanting polished modern comfort.
A bohemian nightlife and arts district at the foot of San Cristobal hill, colorful and lively with Pablo Neruda's house and bustling bars; suits younger travelers and night owls.
A leafy, exclusive residential district in the northeast with designer boutiques, fine dining and parks; suits affluent visitors seeking quiet luxury.
A laid-back middle-class residential district with plazas and a strong cafe and bar scene around Plaza Nunoa; suits travelers wanting an authentic, less touristy neighborhood feel.

water.note: Tap water is treated and safe to drink; may have a strong mineral or chlorine taste.

transit.pay: You need a rechargeable Tarjeta bip! card for both Metro and Red buses (cash is not accepted onboard); buy and load it at metro station machines, kiosks or partner stores. Fares run about CLP 700-830 (~$0.75-0.90) depending on time of day, with free transfers within a set window.
transit.hours: The Metro runs about 6am-11pm weekdays (later start on Sundays/holidays); Red buses run 24 hours with reduced night service.

transit.m: Centropuerto bus to Los Heroes/center, ~40 min
Airport bus plus Metro Line 1, ~1 hr

food.name: Empanada de pino
food.desc: Baked pastry filled with minced beef, onion, a black olive, raisins and half a hard-boiled egg. Chile's national snack, biggest in September.

places.name: Emporio Zunino
places.note: Long-standing empanada counter beside the Mercado; a Santiago rite of passage.

places.name: El Rapido
places.note: Classic stand-up spot near Plaza de Armas serving empanadas and completos since the 1930s.

places.name: San Camilo
places.note: Local bakery chain with around 60 branches, consistently rated for good, cheap empanadas.

food.name: Pastel de choclo
food.desc: Beef, chicken, olive and egg baked under a lid of ground sweetcorn and basil, browned with sugar. Served in a clay dish, mostly in summer.

places.name: Galindo
places.note: Neighbourhood picada repeatedly named by food critics for its pastel de choclo.

places.name: Hosteria Dona Tina
places.note: Countryside-style institution on the city's eastern edge; worth the taxi for traditional cooking.

places.name: Liguria
places.note: Beloved bar-restaurant chain doing Chilean classics with a buzzing after-work crowd.

food.name: Completo
food.desc: A Chilean hot dog buried under diced tomato, sauerkraut and a mountain of avocado and mayonnaise. Ask for the italiano for the flag's colours.

places.name: Domino
places.note: The reference chain since 1952; fast counter service and the standard by which others are judged.

places.name: El Rapido
places.note: Old-school stand-up counter serving completos alongside its famous empanadas.

places.name: Bellavista carts
places.note: Late-night completo stands feeding the bar crowd until the early hours.

food.name: Chorrillana
food.desc: A platter of fries buried under grilled beef, caramelised onion and fried eggs, meant to be shared over beer by three or four people.

places.name: Liguria
places.note: Reliable full-size chorrillana in a lively Chilean bar-restaurant; go hungry and share.

places.name: Bellavista bars
places.note: Night-owl territory for chorrillanas, completos and pisco sours until very late.

places.name: Dulce Pimienta
places.note: Serves an enormous chorrillana mixta with caramelised onion under layers of grilled meats.

food.name: Churrasco italiano and lomito
food.desc: Thin grilled beef or sliced pork loin in a soft roll, loaded with mashed avocado, tomato and mayonnaise. Chile's great sandwich tradition.

places.name: Fuente Alemana
places.note: Horseshoe counter serving vast sandwiches since 1954; eat standing and take napkins.

places.name: Elkika
places.note: No-frills sandwich counter popular with office workers at lunchtime.

places.name: Liguria
places.note: Sit-down version of the classics with a proper Chilean bar atmosphere.

food.name: Seafood and caldillo de congrio
food.desc: Chile's cold Pacific delivers machas, erizos and congrio eel, the last stewed into the caldillo Pablo Neruda wrote an ode to.

places.name: Mercado Central
places.note: Historic iron-roofed fish market ringed with seafood restaurants; go at lunch, not dinner.

places.name: La Vega Chica
places.note: Market food stalls across the river where locals eat cheaply and very well.

places.name: Galindo
places.note: Traditional picada that also does Chilean seafood staples without the market markup.

food.name: Terremoto
food.desc: Sweet young white wine topped with grenadine or fernet and a scoop of pineapple ice cream. The second glass is called a replica, an aftershock.

places.name: La Piojera
places.note: The legendary guachaca bar behind Mercado Central where the drink was popularised; take a taxi at night.

places.name: El Hoyo
places.note: Century-old picada famous for terremotos and chicha, plus hearty Chilean plates.

places.name: Bellavista bars
places.note: Nearly every bar in the barrio pours one; a gentler introduction than La Piojera.

food.name: Mote con huesillo
food.desc: A summer street drink of dried peach stewed in spiced sugar syrup, poured over husked wheat. Sold from carts and drunk with a spoon.

places.name: El Rey del Mote con Huesillo
places.note: Dedicated shop known for generous portions at low prices; the connoisseur's choice.

places.name: Cerro San Cristobal carts
places.note: Reward at the top of the funicular, with the whole city spread out below.

places.name: Parque Forestal and Plaza de Armas carts
places.note: Street carts through the summer months; the most everyday way to try it.

landmarks: Cerro San Cristóbal
Santiago's highest hill, topped by a giant statue of the Virgin Mary and reachable by funicular, offering the best panoramic city views.
Plaza de Armas
The historic founding square of Santiago, ringed by colonial-era buildings and the Metropolitan Cathedral, alive with street life.
Palacio de La Moneda
Chile's neoclassical presidential palace, notable for its ceremonial changing of the guard and role in national history.
Gran Torre Santiago (Costanera Center)
The tallest skyscraper in Latin America, its Sky Costanera observation deck gives sweeping views over the Andes and city.
Cerro Santa Lucía
A picturesque hill park with ornate terraces, fountains and castle-like structures right in the heart of downtown Santiago.
Santiago Metropolitan Cathedral
The grand neoclassical cathedral anchoring Plaza de Armas, seat of the Archdiocese of Santiago and a key architectural landmark.
Museum of Memory and Human Rights
A striking modern museum documenting the Pinochet-era human rights abuses, both architecturally bold and historically significant.
Mercado Central
A beautiful 19th-century cast-iron market hall famous for fresh seafood restaurants, popular with photographers for its ornate structure.
Barrio Lastarria
A charming bohemian neighborhood of cobblestone streets, cafes and galleries, prized for its picturesque architecture.
Chilean National Museum of Fine Arts
An elegant Beaux-Arts palace housing Chile's premier art collection, notable for its grand glass-domed central hall.

train.note: No international passenger trains run from Santiago. EFE runs domestic services south from Estacion Central to Nos, Rancagua, Talca and Chillan.

bus.note: International coaches cross the Andes from Santiago's Terminal Sur / Terminal Alameda to Mendoza and Buenos Aires (Argentina), with some services to Lima, Peru. The high mountain pass can close in winter (roughly Jun-Sep) after snow, so check before travelling and carry your passport.

ferry.note: Santiago is inland; its nearest ports (Valparaiso, San Antonio) handle cruise and cargo, not scheduled passenger ferries. Chile's famous Navimag ferry through the Patagonian fjords runs far to the south, from Puerto Montt to Puerto Natales (https://www.navimag.com/) - all domestic.

half.name: Valparaíso
half.blurb: Colorful hillside port city famed for its funiculars, street art and bohemian character.

half.name: Viña del Mar
half.blurb: Breezy seaside resort town with sandy beaches, gardens and its landmark flower clock.

half.name: Cajón del Maipo
half.blurb: Scenic mountain canyon with hot springs, hiking trails and a turquoise glacial reservoir.

half.name: Maipo Valley
half.blurb: Renowned wine country of vineyards and cellars producing Chile's celebrated Cabernet Sauvignon reds.

half.name: Casablanca Valley
half.blurb: Cool coastal wine valley known for crisp white wines and welcoming vineyard estates.

half.name: Valle Nevado
half.blurb: High Andean ski resort with sweeping mountain views and slopes above the treeline.
